title: Behold the man (John 18:39–19:16)
hook: purple robe, thorns, and Pilate's words: behold the man

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pilate asked what is truth, and walked out before the answer. Your line: I find in him no fault at all.

A crown of thorns. A purple cloak. A Roman official beside a beaten man, one hand stretched toward him, as if presenting him to a crowd below. Sometimes the prisoner holds a reed like a scepter. Sometimes the crowd is painted in, shouting. Painters have come back to this scene for more than five hundred years, and many of the paintings carry the same two-word Latin title.

Pilate offers the crowd a choice: there's a custom of releasing one prisoner at Passover. Shall I release the King of the Jews? They shout for Barabbas instead, and John adds four words: "Now Barabbas was a robber." Then Pilate has Jesus scourged. Roman soldiers twist thorns into a crown, throw on him a purple robe, the color of emperors, and mock him: hail, King. They strike him. Then Pilate brings him out. In the King James Bible: "Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And Pilate saith unto them, Behold the man!" In Latin, Ecce homo. Why does Pilate say it? Perhaps he means, look, he's harmless, he's been punished enough. Perhaps it's contempt. The text doesn't say. But John's readers have heard more than Pilate could have meant: here is what a human being looks like, stripped, mocked, and still standing. Many Christians hear in it every person ever beaten, humiliated or put on display, and God standing with them. The scene tightens. Pilate says again, I find no fault in him. The chief priests cry, crucify him. Pilate is afraid and tries once more to release him. Then they warn him that letting this man go would make him no friend of Caesar. Near noon, Pilate brings Jesus out a last time: behold your King. The chief priests answer, we have no king but Caesar. Then Pilate, the Roman governor, hands him over to be crucified by Roman soldiers.

Bring to mind one person who is suffering right now, someone you know or a face from the news you scrolled past. Don't analyze it or fix it; just look, notice the urge to glance away, and stay a little longer. If you pray, hold that person before God in silence; if not, simply let them be seen by you.
Ecce homo. Latin for behold the man: Pilate's words as he brings out Jesus, crowned with thorns and robed in purple.
Your line: stripped, mocked, and still standing. Rest now; tomorrow, a robe with no seam.

howItsDone: Christians remember this scene in Holy Week and in the Stations of the Cross, and in Jerusalem pilgrims walking the Via Dolorosa pass a Roman-era arch known as the Ecce Homo Arch.

original.note: Greek: behold the man. in the Latin Vulgate, ecce homo.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate is pointing out the prisoner.
what it means: a beaten man in a mock king's robe is put on display, and readers have seen in him every suffering human being.
what a scholar hears: ecce homo, from Jerome's Latin. the 'Ecce Homo Arch' in Jerusalem is usually dated to a Roman building phase about a century after Jesus.

chat.says: So many paintings are called Ecce Homo. What does it mean, and who said it?
options: It's Latin for behold the man: Pilate, presenting Jesus in thorns and purple.
It's Latin for here is the king: the crowd, welcoming Jesus into Jerusalem.
It's Latin for behold the lamb: John the Baptist, seeing Jesus by the river.
chat.meaning: In John 19:5, Pilate brings Jesus out in the crown of thorns and purple robe and says, Behold the man! In Latin, Ecce homo.

Barabbas.meaning: the prisoner the crowd chose; John calls him a robber
